Watching Someone You Love Struggle Can Bring Up A Strong Urge To Step In And Make Things Better

And sometimes, that urge isn’t just about helping them.
It’s also about how uncomfortable it feels to sit with their pain.

But not everything needs to be fixed immediately.

Some processes take their own time.
And being present, without rushing to solve, can be just as important.

Why " We Need To Talk " Fills You With Dread

"We need to talk" shouldn't feel like a warning.

But when conflict at home was loud, unpredictable, or emotionally unsafe, the nervous system learned to treat it that way.

Some things take a long time to unlearn.

Explore the post—tap “Learn More”.

The Real Reason Queer People Face Mental Health Struggles
Being queer is not a mental health condition.

The distress that queer people experience isn’t caused by being queer. It’s caused by what the world makes of it. The rejection, the concealment, the hypervigilance, the accumulation of being made to feel like you are too much or not enough or simply wrong.

Those are the things that cause harm.

In this conversation, we explore what it actually means to walk into mental health care as a queer person, and why the distinction between identity and experience matters so much in the room.

Head to YouTube to watch the full conversation.

Explore the post—tap “Learn More”

Why People Confuse Sex, Gender And Identity

Most people use sex, gender, and sexual orientation interchangeably. They're three distinct things.

Understanding the difference between these three things changes a lot. About how you see yourself. About how you see other people. About why the conversation around identity is more layered than most of us were taught.

In this conversation, we explore what identity actually means, and why collapsing it into a single category leaves so much of the experience unspoken.

Explore the post—tap “Learn More”.

Can Privacy Exist In Healthy Relationship?

Healthy relationships need honesty, but honesty doesn’t always mean immediate or total disclosure.

You’re allowed to process parts of your mental health privately before sharing them. Emotional boundaries are not automatically emotional avoidance.

We often treat openness as an all-or-nothing concept, but emotional safety matters too. Taking time to understand your thoughts, feelings, or triggers before talking about them isn't dishonesty—it's self-awareness.

As Sweta Bothra, Director of Psychology Services at Amaha, reminds us, vulnerability isn't about having no boundaries. It's about sharing from a place of clarity rather than pressure.

3 Ways Grief Comes Back After Loosing A Parent

Why does grief come back years later and feel completely different from the first time?

Here's what no one prepares you for.

Explore the post—tap “Learn More”.

How To Tell A Parent You're Going To Therapy, Without It Turning Into A Fight

"Kya humne kuch galat kiya?"

That's usually where this conversation ends up.

Telling an Indian parent you're going to therapy is its own kind of therapy. Here's how you can navigate it, from the first mention to the moment it gets hard.

Has Your Nervous System Been Trying To Get Your Attention?

The body keeps a record of everything the mind doesn't get a chance to process.

Stress, grief, anxiety, or unresolved things, they don't just disappear because you pushed through them. The body is almost always the first place they show up.

The Biggest Risk With Psychiatric Medications Happens When Someone Starts To Feel Better

A lot of people stop medication when they start feeling better. But psychiatric medication doesn't work that way.

The absence of symptoms is not the same as recovery, and this distinction matters.

Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) doesn’t always look like visible rituals
Sometimes, OCD shows up as intrusive thoughts that feel difficult or even impossible to talk about.

These thoughts can centre around harm, religion, or sexuality—often distressing because they go directly against a person’s values.

They’re commonly accompanied by intense guilt, shame, and anxiety, leading people to question their character or keep these experiences to themselves.

But intrusive thoughts in OCD are not a reflection of who someone is.

They are a recognised and well-documented part of the condition.

Understanding this can help reduce shame and make it easier to seek mental health support, therapy, and treatment for OCD.

If this resonates, it might help to know that you’re not alone.

Developing positive coping skills may involve learning techniques for emotional regulation, problem-solving, communication, mindfulness, and stress management. These skills can help improve resilience, support mental well-being, and promote healthier responses to difficult situations. 

Professional psychological support can help individuals identify unhelpful patterns and build practical strategies tailored to their unique needs and goals. Seeking guidance is not only beneficial during times of distress but can also support personal growth and long-term emotional health.

These situations can sometimes lead to stress, sadness, anxiety, or difficulty coping with daily routines. 

Understanding Life Transitions and Adjustment Disorders is important, as emotional responses to change vary from person to person. While many individuals adapt over time, some may experience persistent distress that affects their well-being and functioning. 

Consultation with a qualified Psychology specialist in Mumbai is recommended for proper evaluation and support. A detailed psychological assessment helps identify emotional challenges and provides clarity on coping patterns and stress responses. 

Management of Life Transitions and Adjustment Disorders typically involves supportive counselling, stress management techniques, and developing healthy coping strategies. Therapy focuses on improving emotional resilience and helping individuals adjust to new circumstances in a balanced manner.

Psychosis is a mental health condition in which an individual may experience difficulty distinguishing between what is real and what is not. Symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions, confused thinking, changes in behaviour, and difficulty concentrating. These experiences can be distressing for both individuals and their families, but early recognition and professional support can make a meaningful difference. 

Psychosis may occur in association with various mental health conditions, severe stress, certain medical conditions, or substance use. Seeking timely psychological assessment is important to understand the underlying factors and determine the most appropriate care pathway. 

A comprehensive approach to Psychosis often includes psychological support, coping strategies, family education, and collaboration with other healthcare professionals when needed. Ongoing care can help improve daily functioning, strengthen support systems, and enhance overall quality of life. 

At Dr. Rochelle Gomes' Psychology clinic in Mumbai, individuals experiencing symptoms of psychosis receive compassionate, patient-centred care in a respectful and non-judgemental environment. The clinic focuses on evidence-based psychological support, education, and personalised guidance to help individuals and families navigate mental health challenges with understanding, dignity, and hope.

Personality disorders are mental health conditions that affect the way a person thinks, feels, and behaves in long-term patterns that may differ from cultural expectations. These patterns can influence relationships, work life, emotional regulation, and overall well-being.

Individuals with personality disorders may experience difficulties in managing emotions, maintaining stable relationships, or adapting to everyday social situations. Symptoms and their intensity can vary widely depending on the type of condition and individual circumstances.

Early recognition and professional psychological support are important for better understanding and management. A structured assessment by a qualified psychologist helps in identifying patterns of behavior and planning appropriate therapeutic support.

Management typically involves psychotherapy, emotional regulation strategies, and long-term psychological guidance. With consistent support, individuals can develop healthier coping skills, improve interpersonal relationships, and enhance overall quality of life.

Dr. Rochelle Gomes provides Psychology care in Mumbai with a focus on the assessment and supportive management of Personality Disorders. The approach emphasizes careful evaluation, patient-centered therapy, and evidence-based psychological interventions in a respectful environment.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is a structured form of psychological treatment that helps individuals understand and manage the connection between thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. It is commonly used to address concerns such as stress, anxiety, low mood, and difficulty coping with everyday challenges.

In Psychology practice, CBT focuses on identifying unhelpful thinking patterns and gradually replacing them with more balanced and constructive perspectives. The approach is practical and goal-oriented, often involving guided discussions, self-reflection techniques, and skill-building exercises that support emotional regulation and healthier coping strategies.

Understanding Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) highlights its role in improving mental well-being through consistent practice and professional guidance. It is widely used because it is structured, evidence-informed, and adaptable to individual needs across different age groups.

For individuals seeking CBT in Mumbai, consultation with a qualified Psychology professional is recommended for proper assessment and personalized therapeutic planning. Early support can help individuals develop effective coping skills and improve overall emotional well-being.

At Dr. Rochelle Gomes, Psychology care is focused on structured therapeutic approaches such as CBT, tailored to individual concerns.

Child and adolescent therapy focuses on supporting the emotional, behavioral, and developmental needs of children and teenagers. This form of care helps young individuals navigate challenges such as anxiety, low mood, school-related stress, behavioral difficulties, and changes in family or social environments. 

Early psychological support is important, as emotional concerns during childhood and adolescence can influence learning, relationships, and overall well-being. Therapy provides a safe and structured space where young individuals can express themselves, build coping skills, and develop healthier patterns of thinking and behavior.

When I first started therapy with him, I was in an extremely fragile mental state. I was experiencing schizophrenic-like attacks and hallucinations. My anxiety was so severe that I was scared to step out of my house, scared to take a lift, scared to sit in a car, metro, or any moving vehicle. I was terrified of water bodies, small spaces, and even fears that are hard to explain or imagine. My life felt completely restricted by fear.

We started therapy from that point. It took me some time to understand his working style, but what stood out the most is that he never forces therapy on you. He truly believes that healing happens when you choose it. He creates a space where you arrive at therapy by yourself, in your own readiness, and that philosophy changed everything for me.

Initially, psychodrama was difficult for me because I was very much in my mind, trying to control and intellectualize everything. But as we continued, I slowly built trust, learned to let go, and switched off my analytical mind. That’s when the real transformation began.

What makes Dr. Ghosh different is his deep love and respect for his discipline. I’ve seen him constantly reading, learning, and researching—even between sessions. His commitment to understanding the human mind and trauma at the root level is rare. He doesn’t work on surface symptoms; he always goes to the root cause, and that’s where real healing happens.

My healing journey with him has been incredibly smooth and profound. Today, I can honestly say I’ve reached around 80% of my healing journey, and my entire life has changed. I have worked with multiple therapists before, but he was the last therapist I gave myself a chance with—and it worked in the most magical, almost miraculous way.

If you are looking for help for yourself or a loved one, I highly recommend Dr. Amitabh Ghosh. This is the kind of therapist you should give a genuine try. For me, he has been the best therapeutic guide I’ve ever met.

And if you ever come across this review, I truly believe it’s not a coincidence. Maybe God led you here. Please don’t ignore it—give this a chance.

10/10 recommended.
Love and peace.

owner_posts.post_text: In a world that’s always ‘on,’ the real strength today is knowing when to pause. Feeling mentally drained doesn’t mean you’re failing — it means you’ve been carrying too much for too long. Give yourself permission to rest, unplug, and breathe. Protecting your peace is productivity too.

Summer can affect mental health in different ways. For some people, sunshine and longer days may improve mood. For others, rising temperatures can worsen anxiety, low mood, irritability, fatigue, and poor sleep.

Heat places extra stress on the body, can disturb sleep, and may intensify physical sensations like a racing heart or restlessness, which can feel similar to anxiety. Poor sleep during warmer nights can also affect concentration, emotional balance, and energy levels.

At the same time, simple protective habits can make a real difference: staying hydrated, keeping a regular routine, gentle movement, rest, and spending time in calming natural spaces.

In simple terms: summer can boost mood when the body is well-regulated. Prioritising sleep, hydration, and rest is not just self-care~it is mental health care.

We at Mindsight encourage you to stay hydrated, slow down when needed, and take gentle care of your mind and body this summer. ☀️

Resilience check-in 🌱

Self-Discipline vs Self-Compassion: 

Which one actually helps you stay consistent?

We’re often taught that strict self-discipline and self-criticism are the keys to success. 

But research and clinical experience show that self-compassion—being kind, understanding, and realistic with yourself—actually leads to better consistency over time. 

When you respond to mistakes with curiosity instead of harsh judgment, you reduce shame, build emotional safety, and make it easier to try again.

Self-discipline rooted in self-compassion isn’t about “letting yourself off the hook”; it’s about supporting yourself in a way that makes growth sustainable, not exhausting. 🌱

featured_reviews.name: Nasra A
featured_reviews.review_text:
Honestly, I don’t know how I would’ve gotten through my teenage years without Sonam. She helped me deal with so much—my self-esteem, sadness and just figuring out who I even wanted to be. Her sessions were my safe space where I could just be myself, without feeling judged or like I had to have it all together.

She celebrated every single win with me, no matter how small. Even stuff like just getting out of bed or going outside—she made me feel like those moments mattered. She used these amazing metaphors and analogies to explain things, and somehow, they always made sense. She had a way of pushing me when I needed it, but she also knew when to back off if I couldn’t handle it that day. One thing that she always did was challenge my irrational beliefs and that practice has stuck with me till date.

Looking back, I don’t think I’d be where I am now without her. She helped me see my own worth and made me believe that I could keep going, even when it felt impossible. Out of all the therapists I could have met, I’m glad it was Sonam.
